sections.title: 1. Clinical Overview & NCSBN CJMM Telemetry Cues

blocks.text: The **NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (NCJMM)** is the clinical scoring backbone of the Next-Generation NCLEX-RN (NGN). Instead of testing isolated recall, unfolding 6-item case studies evaluate whether you can notice unstable bedside monitor and lab trends early, connect findings to organ risk, rank life threats, select safe interventions, and verify physiological recovery.

blocks.alt: Real ICU vital signs telemetry monitor paired with the 6-step NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model in Black and Blue
blocks.caption: Figure 1.1: Filtering unstable bedside telemetry cues through the 6-Step NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (Saunders Unit I · Kaplan Ch. 1–3).

blocks.title: NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM)
blocks.caption: Sequential clinical reasoning cycle tested across every NGN unfolding case.

steps.label: Recognize Cues
steps.detail: Identify abnormal vitals, labs & symptom trends vs. normal baseline

steps.label: Analyze Cues
steps.detail: Connect findings to likely complications & underlying pathophysiology

steps.label: Prioritize Hypotheses
steps.detail: Rank immediate airway, breathing & shock threats first

steps.label: Generate Solutions
steps.detail: Select safe bedside orders & flag contraindicated interventions

steps.label: Take Action
steps.detail: Perform the single safest #1 priority bedside intervention first

steps.label: Evaluate Outcomes
steps.detail: Measure post-intervention vitals, labs & clinical stability

sections.title: 2. Step-by-Step Bedside Cue Matrix (What NGN Scores)

blocks.title: NCSBN 6 Cognitive Layers: Bedside Triggers & Exam Rules
rows: **1. Recognize Cues**
"What matters most right now?"
Focus on changing trends: BP dropping from 128/78 to 90/56 while HR climbs 74 -> 118 indicates impending shock rather than benign pain.
**2. Analyze Cues**
"What pathophysiology does this signal?"
Link lab shifts to organ risk: Na+ 121 mEq/L + lethargy -> cerebral edema/seizure risk; K+ 6.4 mEq/L + peaked T waves -> lethal ventricular arrhythmia.
**3. Prioritize Hypotheses**
"Which threat kills first?"
Apply ABCs + Maslow's physiological tier: airway stridor, tension pneumothorax, and sepsis hypotension always precede discharge teaching.
**4. Generate Solutions**
"Which orders help vs. harm?"
Anticipate IV isotonic fluids, oxygen, cultures, and **hold contraindicated orders** (e.g., beta-blockers in bradycardia, K+ in anuria, vaginal exam in placenta previa).
**5. Take Action**
"What single bedside step comes first?"
Act on immediate life support before calling the provider when intervention is clear (raise HOB for acute dyspnea, stop anaphylactic infusion, apply pressure to active arterial bleeding).
**6. Evaluate Outcomes**
"Did the client improve or worsen?"
Verify concrete targets: urine output >= 30 mL/hr post-bolus, crackles clearing after furosemide, glucose > 70 mg/dL post-D50W.

blocks.title: Kaplan & LaCharity Safety Anchor
blocks.text: On NGN bedside dilemmas, NEVER skip physical safety to wait for chart review when an acute ABC threat is evident on assessment—stabilize oxygenation, perfusion, or infusion toxicity first, then notify the provider with complete ISBAR data.

blocks.alt: Real blood pressure bedside verification photo with NGN Bow-Tie item layout, Matrix grid, and +/- partial credit scoring guide
blocks.caption: Figure 1.2: NGN Bow-Tie Architecture, Matrix Indicated/Contraindicated rows, and +/- Partial Credit Scoring Rules.

blocks.title: Next-Generation NCLEX (NGN) Item Formats & Partial-Credit Scoring Rules
rows: **Extended Multiple Response (EMR)**
Choose all clinically safe actions from 5–10 checkboxes.
**+/- Polytomous Scoring:** +1 per correct selection, **-1 per wrong pick** (floor 0). Never guess unsure options.
**Bow-Tie Item**
Pick 1 likely diagnosis (center), 2 actions & 2 monitoring targets.
**0/1 Per Cell:** Solve the **center diagnosis first**, then check left urgent actions and right evaluation targets.
**Matrix / Grid**
Mark each clinical row as **Indicated**, **Contraindicated**, or **Non-Essential**.
Evaluate each row independently against drug allergies, bleeding risk, electrolyte levels, and vitals.
**Highlight & Cloze Drop-Down**
Click abnormal chart spans or complete clinical reasoning dropdowns.
Highlight **only abnormal trends** (rising Cr/lactate, falling SpO2); leave normal baseline text unmarked.

sections.title: 4. Worked NGN Unfolding Case Walkthrough (Post-Op Septic Shock)

blocks.text: Apply all 6 CJMM steps across a classic surgical-unit unfolding deterioration scenario adapted for NGN Bow-Tie and Matrix questions:

blocks.title: Unfolding NGN Case Example: 68-Year-Old Post-Op Colectomy Day 2
rows: **Recognize & Analyze**
Temp 38.9 °C, HR 122 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, RR 28/min, Lactate 4.1 mmol/L, warm flushed skin turning mottled.
Progressive **septic shock** with tissue hypoperfusion and metabolic lactic acidosis.
**Prioritize & Generate**
Orders: (A) NS 30 mL/kg IV bolus, (B) Broad-spectrum antibiotics after blood cultures, (C) Foley catheter I&O, (D) PRN lisinopril 20 mg PO.
**Indicated:** A, B, C (after cultures). **Contraindicated:** Lisinopril (worsens vasodilatory shock).
**Take Action & Evaluate**
Start rapid isotonic NS infusion + oxygen, draw 2 sets blood cultures first, infuse broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.
**Expected Recovery:** MAP >= 65 mmHg, urine output >= 30 mL/hr, lactate trending down.

quiz.prompt: A client managed for NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM) develops sudden tachypnea (RR 32/min), SpO2 87%, and new-onset restlessness. What should the nurse do FIRST?
options: Administer a PRN opioid analgesic for restlessness before assessing.
Document the vital signs and recheck oxygen saturation in 2 hours.
Elevate the head of the bed, assess airway/lung sounds, and apply supplemental oxygen.
Ask the UAP to assist the client to ambulate in the hallway.
quiz.rationale: Under Maslow's hierarchy and ABC prioritization in NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM), airway and oxygenation cues (SpO2 87%, RR 32, hypoxia-induced restlessness) require immediate airway/O2 support first.

quiz.prompt: Which client care task related to NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM) is appropriate to delegate to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel (UAP)?
options: Obtaining routine vital signs and strictly measuring oral intake and urine output on a stable client.
Evaluating the client's therapeutic response to an intravenous high-alert medication.
Performing the comprehensive admission assessment for a newly arrived acute client.
Providing initial discharge teaching on red-flag warning signs.
quiz.rationale: Per LaCharity PDA and NCSBN delegation rules, UAPs perform routine, stable data collection (vitals, I&O, ADLs), while assessment, teaching, and evaluation remain RN-only duties.

quiz.prompt: A preceptor reviews discharge teaching for a client recovering under NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM). Which statement by the client indicates teaching was effective?
options: "It is fine to take over-the-counter NSAIDs alongside my prescribed anticoagulants without asking."
"Once I feel a little better tomorrow, I can stop taking all prescribed medications."
"I do not need follow-up lab monitoring because my hospital discharge labs were normal."
"I will monitor for warning signs like fever, worsening shortness of breath, or bleeding and contact my provider promptly."
quiz.rationale: Effective client education in NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Measurement Model (CJMM) requires adherence to therapy, scheduled lab follow-ups, and prompt reporting of acute deterioration.

quiz.prompt: When using the NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Model (CJMM) for a client in Course Unit 1: Next-Generation NCLEX (NGN), Clinical Judgment & Test-Taking Strategies, what directly follows 'Recognize Cues' and 'Analyze Cues'?
options: Evaluate Outcomes prior to implementing any bedside intervention.
Archive the admission chart without creating a care plan.
Prioritize Hypotheses — ranking immediate life-threatening complications first.
Delegate hypothesis ranking to support staff before completing assessment.
quiz.rationale: The 6 steps of the NCSBN CJMM progress in order: Recognize Cues -> Analyze Cues -> Prioritize Hypotheses -> Generate Solutions -> Take Action -> Evaluate Outcomes.

quiz.prompt: A patient is experiencing vertigo. The nurse knows that this symptom is likely related to a problem with what part of the sensory system?
options: Visual system
Vestibular system
Olfactory system
Tactile system
quiz.rationale: The vestibular system (B), located within the inner ear, is responsible for maintaining balance and spatial orientation. Vertigo, a sensation of feeling off balance, is often caused by problems in this system. The visual (A), olfactory (C), and tactile (D) systems are not typically associated with symptoms of vertigo.

quiz.prompt: As a nurse leader, you notice that one of your team members is consistently late for their shift. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ignore the behavior as it doesn't affect patient care.
Report the behavior to the hospital administration.
Discuss the issue with the team member privately.
Publicly reprimand the team member during a staff meeting.
quiz.rationale: In this situation, the most appropriate action for a nurse leader is to address the issue directly with the individual involved (C). Ignoring the behavior (A) is not an effective leadership strategy as it fails to address the issue. Reporting the behavior to administration (B) should be a last resort if the behavior continues after addressing it directly. Publicly reprimanding the team member (D) is not appropriate and could create a hostile work environment.

quiz.prompt: As a nurse leader, you are implementing a change in a hospital protocol. What is the best way to ensure staff compliance with this change?
options: Enforce strict punishments for non-compliance.
Communicate the rationale for the change.
Make the change without explaining why.
Implement the change without seeking staff input.
quiz.rationale: Effective leadership involves open and clear communication. Explaining the rationale for the change (B) helps staff understand the importance and necessity of the change, thereby fostering compliance. Enforcing strict punishments (A) tends to create a negative work environment. Implementing a change without explanation (C) or without seeking staff input (D) can lead to resistance and non-compliance.

quiz.prompt: A nurse is teaching a patient who has been diagnosed with glaucoma. Which of the following statements by the patient indicates the need for further teaching?
options: "I will need to use my eye drops daily."
"I will avoid straining during bowel movements."
"I am glad I can stop taking my eye drops once my symptoms improve."
"I understand that I will need regular check-ups for my eye pressure."
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: "I am glad I can stop taking my eye drops once my symptoms improve." (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: A nurse is providing leadership training to a group of new graduate nurses. Which of the following leadership styles is likely to be most effective for promoting autonomy and critical thinking among the new nurses?
options: Autocratic
Laissez-faire
Democratic
Transactional
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: Democratic (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: A nurse is assessing a patient with suspected macular degeneration. Which of the following findings would most likely indicate this condition?
options: Loss of peripheral vision
Difficulty distinguishing colors
Blurred vision
Central vision loss
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: Central vision loss (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

sections.title: 1. Clinical Overview & NCLEX-RN Computer Adaptive Testing (CAT)

blocks.text: The **NCLEX-RN Computerized Adaptive Test (CAT)** continuously recalculates your clinical competency logit estimate after every single response. Passing requires demonstrating with **95% statistical confidence** that your ability exceeds the NCSBN passing standard within **85 to 150 questions** (maximum **5 hours**, including 15 unscored pretest items). Internationally educated nurses (IENs) must also master converting SI lab values (`mmol/L`) and BAN/rINN drug names into **US Conventional units (`mg/dL`, `mEq/L`)** and **USAN nomenclature**.

blocks.alt: Real nurse study cohort photo with CAT adaptive logit trajectory curve and NCSBN Client Needs blueprint percentages
blocks.caption: Figure 1.3: NCLEX-RN Computer Adaptive Testing (CAT) Logit Stopping Rule & NCSBN Client Needs Exam Weights.

blocks.title: NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan — Client Needs Blueprint Weights
rows: **Management of Care**
Delegation (RN vs. LPN vs. UAP), Client Rights, Informed Consent, HIPAA, Prioritization & Case Management.
**Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies**
High-alert IV medications (Insulin, Heparin, Warfarin, Digoxin, Potassium), blood transfusions, TPN & central lines.
**Physiological Adaptation**
ICU/ED acute instability: sepsis, shock, DKA/HHS, acute MI, respiratory failure & ABG acid-base emergencies.
**Safety & Infection Control**
Transmission precautions (Airborne/Droplet/Contact), fire RACE/PASS, restraint safety & incident reporting.
**Reduction of Risk Potential**
US Conventional lab values (BMP, CBC, Coags), vital-sign shifts, endoscopy/catheter pre/post-procedure safety.
**Health Promotion & Psychosocial**
6% – 12% each
US CDC vaccine schedules, cancer screening, therapeutic communication, abuse reporting & crisis intervention.

sections.title: 2. International Nurse Licensure Pathway, Fees & Work Visas

blocks.alt: US clinical orientation photography with CGFNS CES verification, State Board fees, Pearson VUE ATT, and EB-3 vs H-1B comparison
blocks.caption: Figure 1.4: Foreign-Trained Nurse Registration Portals, Official Fee Benchmarks & US Employment Visa Pathways.

blocks.title: Foreign-Trained RN Registration Steps, Official Portals & Work Visa Tracks
rows: **01. Eligibility & Records**
Diploma or BScN + Home Council (2yr bedside exp ideal)
Active, unencumbered nursing license from home council (e.g., UNMC/NCK/NMC); nursing school & council must dispatch transcripts directly.
**02. CGFNS Verification**
CGFNS Credentials Evaluation Service (CES ~**$485**)
Candidate uploads secondary certificates; home school and regulatory board send official syllabi and verification forms straight to CGFNS.
**03. State Board & Prints**
BON (e.g., Texas TBON ~**$75**) + IdentoGO (~**$40**)
Open State Board of Nursing account, complete background check/fingerprinting, and satisfy English exemption or IELTS/OET if required by board.
**04. Pearson VUE & ATT**
Pearson VUE (**$200** exam + ~$150 intl surcharge)
Receive Authorization to Test (ATT), book at Pearson VUE test center, sit 85–150 NGN CAT items.
**EB-3 vs. H-1B Visas**
Direct Hospital Hire or Staffing Agency Sponsor
**EB-3 (Permanent Green Card):** Diploma or BSN eligible; spouse gets open work permit & children attend US schools. **H-1B:** BSN min., employer-tied, spouse restricted.

sections.title: 3. Critical Transition: SI Units & British Drugs -> US NCLEX Standards

blocks.text: NCLEX-RN tests exclusively in **US Conventional Laboratory Units** and **US Adopted Names (USAN)** for medications. Missing a unit shift between `mmol/L` and `mg/dL` or mistaking Paracetamol/Adrenaline terminology costs critical exam points.

blocks.title: Essential Unit & Drug Name Translations for International NCLEX Candidates
rows: **Blood Glucose (Fasting)**
3.9 – 5.5 mmol/L (Urgent low < 3.9)
**70 – 99 mg/dL** (Hypoglycemia < 70 mg/dL; DKA > 250 mg/dL)
**Serum Creatinine / BUN**
Creatinine 62 – 106 µmol/L · Urea 2.5 – 6.7 mmol/L
Creatinine **0.7 – 1.2 mg/dL** · BUN **10 – 20 mg/dL**
**Potassium (K+) & Sodium (Na+)**
Same mEq/L / mmol/L (K+ 3.5–5.0; Na+ 135–145)
**Hemoglobin (Adult)**
Female 120–150 g/L · Male 135–175 g/L
**High-Yield USAN Drug Names**
Paracetamol · Adrenaline · Salbutamol · Pethidine · Frusemide
**Acetaminophen** · **Epinephrine** · **Albuterol** · **Meperidine** · **Furosemide**

blocks.title: 24-Week Cohort Study Cadence (Saunders + Kaplan + LaCharity)
blocks.text: Follow the three-phase progression: master core organ pathophysiology in **Saunders 9th Ed.** (Weeks 1–14), apply structured elimination rules with **Kaplan Decision Trees** (Weeks 15–18), and drill daily **LaCharity PDA** delegation/prioritization plus timed full CAT simulations (Weeks 19–24) before scheduling your ATT exam date.

sections.title: 1. Kaplan 5-Step Decision Tree & Bedside Safety Frameworks

blocks.text: On the Next-Gen NCLEX-RN, clinical knowledge alone will not save you when two or three options look clinically appropriate. Mastering the **Kaplan 5-Step Decision Tree**, **Maslow's Physiological Hierarchy**, **ABCs (Airway -> Breathing -> Circulation)**, and **Acute vs. Chronic Priority Rules** ensures you systematically eliminate distractors and pick the safest first bedside nursing action.

blocks.alt: Real clinician assessment photo paired with ABCs Maslow bedside rescue pyramid and Stable vs Unstable priority rules
blocks.caption: Figure 1.5: Clinical Prioritization Pyramid (ABCs -> Maslow -> Acute vs. Chronic Instability) and the Assess-First Exception Rule.

blocks.title: Kaplan 5-Step NCLEX Question Decision Tree
blocks.caption: Apply in strict sequence whenever multiple options seem clinically reasonable.

steps.label: Identify Topic & Issue
steps.detail: Re-read the final question sentence—what clinical outcome is tested?

steps.label: Assess vs. Implement
steps.detail: Gather physical assessment cues BEFORE calling provider unless emergency rescue needed

steps.label: Maslow & ABCs Filter
steps.detail: Airway obstruction, hypoxia, shock, and acute safety beat routine teaching or psychosocial comfort

steps.label: Outcome of Each Option
steps.detail: Test drug safety holds (HR <60, K+ <3.5, RR <12) & verify bedside protection

steps.label: Confirm Question Fit
steps.detail: Re-read chosen answer back into step 1 to verify zero contraindications

sections.title: 2. Therapeutic Communication, Medication Holds & Priority Scenarios

blocks.alt: Real registered nurse in blue uniform during patient consultation with Kaplan 5-step decision tree and medication safety hold thresholds
blocks.caption: Figure 1.6: Therapeutic Communication Golden Rules, High-Alert Medication Hold Limits & Distractor Elimination.

blocks.title: Saunders & Kaplan High-Yield Question Pattern Matrix
rows: **Assess vs. Call Provider**
Check apical HR, lung sounds, SpO2, pain/swelling or bladder scan BEFORE notifying physician.
'Notify the healthcare provider immediately' when physical vital signs haven't been checked yet.
**Acute Emergency Exception**
Stop blood transfusion for hives/chills, apply O2 for SpO2 84%, clear airway for stridor FIRST.
'Assess IV patency for 15 minutes' during anaphylaxis or delayed airway support.
**Therapeutic Communication**
Reflect emotions ('You seem frightened...'), open-ended prompt, offer silent presence.
Asking **'Why?'**, giving false reassurance ('Everything will be fine'), or passing blame ('Ask your doctor').
**High-Alert Drug Hold Thresholds**
Hold Digoxin/Metoprolol if HR <60; Loop diuretics if K+ <3.5; ACEi if K+ >5.0; Opioids if RR <12; MgSO4 if DTR absent.
Administering unsafe dose anyway and charting 'will monitor closely'.
**Least Invasive -> Most Invasive**
Elevate HOB, cough/deep breath, bladder scan, verbal de-escalation BEFORE suction, Foley, PRN haloperidol or restraints.
Applying physical restraints or chemical sedation as a first-line measure.

items: **Opposites Attract Strategy:** When two single-choice answers express direct medical opposites (e.g., *Monitor for hyperkalemia* vs. *Monitor for hypokalemia*), the core mechanism almost always points toward one of those two.

**Equal Options Cancel Out:** If Option B and Option C mean clinically the same thing on a single-choice question (e.g., *Reduce dietary sodium* vs. *Avoid canned/processed salty foods*), neither can be the single right answer.

**Compound Choice Verification Rule:** If an answer contains multiple symptoms, teachings, or actions linked by 'and', **every single part** must be clinically true—one false clause disqualifies the whole option.

**Eliminate Absolute Language:** Reject 'Always', 'Never', 'Every', 'Only', or 'All clients' unless referring to immutable physical safety absolutes (e.g., never recap contaminated needles, never give KCl IV push).

**Unstable Before Stable Rule:** On priority triage stems, always see acute airway distress, new post-op bleeding, compartment syndrome (unrelieved pain despite opioids), or sudden confusion before routine wound dressing or stable chronic arthritis.

blocks.title: Worked Test-Taking Strategy Vignettes (Master-Study Drills)
rows: **Post-Op Total Knee Replacement (Day 0)** reports sudden calf tenderness & tight warm swelling.
A. Massage calf gently · B. Measure calf & assess pedal pulses · C. Notify provider now · D. Apply heat pack
**B wins:** Assess vascular perfusion & DVT signs first before reporting (**Never massage calf** = PE embolus risk!).
**Blood Transfusion (Packed RBCs)** develops sudden low back pain, chills & hives 10 mins in.
A. Slow infusion rate · B. Administer diphenhydramine first · C. Stop transfusion immediately & keep line open with NS
**C wins:** Emergency exception — stop the infusion immediately with new saline tubing to halt hemolytic/anaphylactic exposure.
**Pre-Op Cataract Client** asks: 'Will my vision definitely come back 100%?'
A. 'Why are you worrying about that?' · B. 'Of course, everyone recovers fully.' · C. 'Tell me what concerns you most about the surgery.'
**C wins:** Open-ended therapeutic exploration of feelings without false reassurance ('Of course') or probing ('Why?').

blocks.title: Don't Panic On Unfamiliar Drug/Disease Terms
blocks.text: When the CAT engine presents an unfamiliar medication or rare condition above passing logit level, **decode the Greek/Latin suffix** (`-olol`, `-pril`, `-sartan`, `-mycin`), apply the **patient's presenting symptom & organ risk**, protect **Airway/Safety**, and never guess blindly on +/- SATA checkboxes.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient who had a laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) procedure. Which of the following is a priority nursing responsibility in the immediate postoperative period?
options: Encouraging the patient to blink frequently
Assisting the patient with ambulation
Protecting the patient’s eyes from injury
Administering antibiotic eye drops
questions.rationale: After LASIK surgery, it's crucial to protect the eyes from any potential injury. The patient's corneas have been reshaped and need time to heal. While administering antibiotic eye drops is also important, it is not the immediate priority.

questions.prompt: The nurse notes continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber of a patient's chest tube drainage system. What should the nurse do?
options: Clamp the chest tube
Assess for a leak in the system
Document the finding as normal
Increase the suction
questions.rationale: Continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber indicates a possible air leak in the system. The nurse should assess the chest tube, connections, and drainage system for leaks.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to administer a bronchodilator to a client with asthma. Which of the following outcomes would indicate that the medication has been effective?
options: The client's pulse oximetry reading is 92%
The client is able to speak in full sentences
The client's respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute
The client's peak flow reading has decreased
questions.rationale: The ability to speak in full sentences without becoming short of breath indicates that the bronchodilator is effective and the client's airway obstruction is improving.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient with pneumonia. The nurse notes decreased breath sounds in the lower lobes of both lungs. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Administering a bronchodilator
Initiating oxygen therapy
Performing chest physiotherapy
Assisting with endotracheal intubation
questions.rationale: Decreased breath sounds in the bases of the lungs indicate mucus accumulation, which can be mobilized with chest physiotherapy.

questions.prompt: A patient with diabetes is experiencing symptoms of hyperglycemia. What is the nurse's first action?
options: Administer insulin
Check blood glucose levels
Encourage fluid intake
Provide emotional support
questions.rationale: Administering insulin helps lower blood glucose levels.

questions.prompt: A client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) has been prescribed ipratropium bromide. What is the primary action of this medication?
options: Decreases inflammation in the airways
Causes bronchodilation
Thins respiratory secretions
Suppresses the cough reflex
questions.rationale: Ipratropium bromide is an anticholinergic bronchodilator. It works by blocking the action of acetylcholine in bronchial smooth muscle, resulting in bronchodilation.

questions.prompt: The parents of a 2-year-old child with short bowel syndrome are concerned about their child's nutrition. Which of the following is an appropriate recommendation by the nurse?
options: The child should consume a high-fiber diet.
The child may require parenteral nutrition.
The child should avoid all fats in the diet.
The child should consume more dairy products.
questions.rationale: Short bowel syndrome can lead to malabsorption of nutrients. In severe cases, parenteral nutrition may be required to ensure the child receives adequate nutrition. A high-fiber diet (option A) may not be appropriate as it can increase stool output. Avoiding all fats (option C) is not recommended as some fat is necessary for growth and development. While some children with short bowel syndrome may tolerate dairy products (option D), others may not due to lactose intolerance.

questions.prompt: A patient is admitted with a pulmonary embolism. Which of the following is the priority nursing intervention?
options: Administer anticoagulant therapy as ordered
Provide supplemental oxygen
Monitor vital signs
Encourage ambulation
questions.rationale: The immediate priority for a patient with a pulmonary embolism is to improve oxygenation, which can be achieved by providing supplemental oxygen.

questions.prompt: A patient with hyperthyroidism is experiencing thyroid storm. What is the nurse's first action?
options: Administer beta blockers
Check thyroid hormone levels
Encourage rest
Provide oxygen therapy
questions.rationale: Beta blockers control symptoms like tachycardia.

questions.prompt: A 5-year-old child weighs 18 kg and is prescribed a medication at a dosage of 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses. The medication comes in a concentration of 40 mg/2 mL. How many milliliters of medication will the nurse administer per dose?
options: 1 mL
2 mL
4.5 mL
9 mL
questions.rationale: Correct answer: 4.5 mL (Verified from PAEDIATRIC QUESTIONS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient post bronchoscopy. Which of the following is the most important assessment before offering the patient food or drink?
options: Vital signs
Oxygen saturation
Level of consciousness
Return of the gag reflex
questions.rationale: After a bronchoscopy, the patient’s throat may be numb from local anaesthetics used during the procedure. It is essential to ensure the return of the gag reflex before offering food or drink to prevent aspiration.

sections.title: 1. US Nursing Legal Standards, Tort Law & Chart Integrity

blocks.text: US state **Nurse Practice Acts** define legal accountability across informed consent, **HIPAA patient privacy**, **Advance Directives**, intentional vs. unintentional torts, physical restraints, and statutory mandatory reporting. On NCLEX-RN Management of Care (`15–21%` test weight), legal safety dilemmas consistently appear as priority actions and matrix items.

blocks.alt: Hospital nursing EHR workstation photo with Informed Consent, HIPAA privacy, Advance Directives and Restraints legal summaries in Black and Blue
blocks.caption: Figure 2.1: Legal Responsibilities of the US Registered Nurse — Informed Consent, HIPAA Confidentiality, Advance Directives & Chart Protection.

blocks.title: Unintentional vs. Intentional Torts & Malpractice Risk
rows: **Negligence / Malpractice** (Unintentional)
Failure to act as a reasonably prudent nurse (Duty -> Breach -> Causation -> Injury).
Failing to put bed alarms up for a dizzy post-op patient resulting in hip fracture; failing to verify allergies before cefazolin.
**Assault** (Intentional)
Threat or attempt to make unwanted physical contact causing fear.
Threatening an uncooperative client: 'If you don't swallow these pills, I will give you an injection instead.'
**Battery** (Intentional)
Actual unconsented touching or performing treatment after refusal.
Inserting a urinary catheter, drawing blood, or giving medication after an alert client explicitly refuses.
**False Imprisonment** (Intentional)
Confining a competent client against their will without legal authority.
Holding an alert voluntary patient who requests **AMA discharge**, or applying restraints strictly for staff convenience.

sections.title: 2. Informed Consent, HIPAA Privacy & Advance Directives

blocks.title: Legal Responsibilities: Consent, Privacy & End-of-Life Orders
rows: **Informed Consent**
Confirm patient is alert, competent, non-medicated & signing voluntarily; witness signature.
RN does **NOT** explain risks, benefits, or surgical alternatives — notify the **performing physician** if the client still has questions.
**HIPAA & Confidentiality**
Limit PHI (verbal, EHR, whiteboards) exclusively to staff directly caring for the patient.
**Never** look up medical records of neighbors, coworkers, or discharged patients you are no longer assigned to care for.
**Advance Directives**
Follow **Living Will** (treatment limits) or **Durable POA / Healthcare Proxy** once client cannot speak.
Most recently dated directive governs; paramedics must initiate resuscitation if signed out-of-hospital DNR is unavailable.
**Incident / Occurrence Reports**
Document purely objective assessment & care in chart; complete internal report separately.
**NEVER write 'Incident report filed'** or 'Nurse forgot dose' in the permanent medical chart.
**Mandatory Reporting**
Legally required reporting even without consent: child/elder abuse, gunshot/stab wounds, TB/STIs.
Report suspected child/vulnerable-adult abuse to CPS/APS immediately — suspicion alone triggers duty to report, not proof.

blocks.title: Restraint Legal Checklist (Saunders Unit II)
blocks.text: Physical/chemical restraints are ALWAYS a last resort after alternatives fail. Obtain a face-to-face provider evaluation within **1 hour** (violent/behavioral), tie quick-release slip knots ONLY to the **moveable bed frame (never side rails)**, inspect skin/circulation every **15–30 minutes**, and release every **2 hours** for toileting and range-of-motion.

quiz.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with Informed Consent (Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
Verify client competence, voluntary agreement & witness signature.
quiz.rationale: For Informed Consent, the priority intervention is: Verify client competence, voluntary agreement & witness signature. Key exam watchpoint: RN does NOT explain procedural risks/alternatives — that is the performing provider's duty.

quiz.prompt: Which statement reflects an unsafe error (or NCLEX trap) that the nurse must AVOID when managing Informed Consent?
options: RN does NOT explain procedural risks/alternatives — that is the performing provider's duty.
Monitor vital signs, airway, and target labs closely during care of Informed Consent.
Use closed-loop SBAR communication when escalating abnormal clinical changes.
Verify client competence, voluntary agreement & witness signature.
quiz.rationale: When caring for Informed Consent, avoiding this unsafe action is critical: RN does NOT explain procedural risks/alternatives — that is the performing provider's duty.

quiz.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with HIPAA & Confidentiality (Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Share chart/PHI only with direct care team; log off unattended screens.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
quiz.rationale: For HIPAA & Confidentiality, the priority intervention is: Share chart/PHI only with direct care team; log off unattended screens. Key exam watchpoint: Do NOT look up charts of family, neighbors, or non-assigned patients out of curiosity.

quiz.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with Incident Reports (Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Document factual care in chart; file internal report separately without bias.
Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
quiz.rationale: For Incident Reports, the priority intervention is: Document factual care in chart; file internal report separately without bias. Key exam watchpoint: Never reference 'Incident Report filed' inside the patient's permanent medical record.

quiz.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with Restraints Safety (Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Obtain provider order (within 1 hr for violent restraints), neurovascular checks q15–30m, release q2h.
Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
quiz.rationale: For Restraints Safety, the priority intervention is: Obtain provider order (within 1 hr for violent restraints), neurovascular checks q15–30m, release q2h. Key exam watchpoint: Never tie restraints to side rails (use quick-release knot on bed frame) or order PRN.

quiz.prompt: A client managed for Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting develops sudden tachypnea (RR 32/min), SpO2 87%, and new-onset restlessness. What should the nurse do FIRST?
options: Ask the UAP to assist the client to ambulate in the hallway.
Elevate the head of the bed, assess airway/lung sounds, and apply supplemental oxygen.
Document the vital signs and recheck oxygen saturation in 2 hours.
Administer a PRN opioid analgesic for restlessness before assessing.
quiz.rationale: Under Maslow's hierarchy and ABC prioritization in Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting, airway and oxygenation cues (SpO2 87%, RR 32, hypoxia-induced restlessness) require immediate airway/O2 support first.

quiz.prompt: Which client care task related to Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting is appropriate to delegate to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel (UAP)?
options: Obtaining routine vital signs and strictly measuring oral intake and urine output on a stable client.
Performing the comprehensive admission assessment for a newly arrived acute client.
Evaluating the client's therapeutic response to an intravenous high-alert medication.
Providing initial discharge teaching on red-flag warning signs.
quiz.rationale: Per LaCharity PDA and NCSBN delegation rules, UAPs perform routine, stable data collection (vitals, I&O, ADLs), while assessment, teaching, and evaluation remain RN-only duties.

quiz.prompt: A preceptor reviews discharge teaching for a client recovering under Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting. Which statement by the client indicates teaching was effective?
options: "I do not need follow-up lab monitoring because my hospital discharge labs were normal."
"Once I feel a little better tomorrow, I can stop taking all prescribed medications."
"It is fine to take over-the-counter NSAIDs alongside my prescribed anticoagulants without asking."
"I will monitor for warning signs like fever, worsening shortness of breath, or bleeding and contact my provider promptly."
quiz.rationale: Effective client education in Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting requires adherence to therapy, scheduled lab follow-ups, and prompt reporting of acute deterioration.

quiz.prompt: When using the NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Model (CJMM) for a client in Course Unit 2: Management of Care — Legal Issues, Ethics, Delegation & Disaster Triage, what directly follows 'Recognize Cues' and 'Analyze Cues'?
options: Archive the admission chart without creating a care plan.
Delegate hypothesis ranking to support staff before completing assessment.
Prioritize Hypotheses — ranking immediate life-threatening complications first.
Evaluate Outcomes prior to implementing any bedside intervention.
quiz.rationale: The 6 steps of the NCSBN CJMM progress in order: Recognize Cues -> Analyze Cues -> Prioritize Hypotheses -> Generate Solutions -> Take Action -> Evaluate Outcomes.

quiz.prompt: A patient is experiencing vertigo. The nurse knows that this symptom is likely related to a problem with what part of the sensory system?
options: Visual system
Vestibular system
Olfactory system
Tactile system
quiz.rationale: The vestibular system (B), located within the inner ear, is responsible for maintaining balance and spatial orientation. Vertigo, a sensation of feeling off balance, is often caused by problems in this system. The visual (A), olfactory (C), and tactile (D) systems are not typically associated with symptoms of vertigo.

quiz.prompt: As a nurse leader, you notice that one of your team members is consistently late for their shift. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ignore the behavior as it doesn't affect patient care.
Report the behavior to the hospital administration.
Discuss the issue with the team member privately.
Publicly reprimand the team member during a staff meeting.
quiz.rationale: In this situation, the most appropriate action for a nurse leader is to address the issue directly with the individual involved (C). Ignoring the behavior (A) is not an effective leadership strategy as it fails to address the issue. Reporting the behavior to administration (B) should be a last resort if the behavior continues after addressing it directly. Publicly reprimanding the team member (D) is not appropriate and could create a hostile work environment.

quiz.prompt: As a nurse leader, you are implementing a change in a hospital protocol. What is the best way to ensure staff compliance with this change?
options: Enforce strict punishments for non-compliance.
Communicate the rationale for the change.
Make the change without explaining why.
Implement the change without seeking staff input.
quiz.rationale: Effective leadership involves open and clear communication. Explaining the rationale for the change (B) helps staff understand the importance and necessity of the change, thereby fostering compliance. Enforcing strict punishments (A) tends to create a negative work environment. Implementing a change without explanation (C) or without seeking staff input (D) can lead to resistance and non-compliance.

quiz.prompt: A nurse is teaching a patient who has been diagnosed with glaucoma. Which of the following statements by the patient indicates the need for further teaching?
options: "I will need to use my eye drops daily."
"I will avoid straining during bowel movements."
"I am glad I can stop taking my eye drops once my symptoms improve."
"I understand that I will need regular check-ups for my eye pressure."
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: "I am glad I can stop taking my eye drops once my symptoms improve." (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: A nurse is providing leadership training to a group of new graduate nurses. Which of the following leadership styles is likely to be most effective for promoting autonomy and critical thinking among the new nurses?
options: Autocratic
Laissez-faire
Democratic
Transactional
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: Democratic (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: A nurse is assessing a patient with suspected macular degeneration. Which of the following findings would most likely indicate this condition?
options: Loss of peripheral vision
Difficulty distinguishing colors
Blurred vision
Central vision loss
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: Central vision loss (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: As a nurse leader, you observe a conflict between two team members. What is the most appropriate initial action?
options: Ignore the conflict and hope it resolves itself.
Immediately report the incident to higher management.
Facilitate a meeting between the two individuals to discuss the issue.
Take sides with the person who has been with the team longer.
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: Facilitate a meeting between the two individuals to discuss the issue. (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: A patient with diabetes reports experiencing numbness and tingling in their feet. This is most likely indicative of which of the following conditions?
options: Diabetic retinopathy
Diabetic neuropathy
Diabetic nephropathy
Diabetic ketoacidosis
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: Diabetic neuropathy (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: A patient with a history of glaucoma has been prescribed eye drops to decrease intraocular pressure. The patient also has other chronic conditions that require medication. Which of the following should be the nurse's priority instruction?
options: "Take your glaucoma eye drops first before any other medication."
"You can take your glaucoma eye drops at the same time as your other medications."
"Take your glaucoma eye drops last after all other medications."
"The timing of your glaucoma eye drops in relation to other medications doesn't matter."
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: "Take your glaucoma eye drops first before any other medication." (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: A nurse is prioritizing care for a patient who has been newly diagnosed with Meniere's disease. Which of the following should be the nurse's first action?
options: Providing patient education about the disease
Starting the patient on a low-sodium diet
Administering prescribed medication
Assessing the patient's current level of knowledge
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: Assessing the patient's current level of knowledge (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

quiz.prompt: A patient with a spinal cord injury report experiencing phantom limb pain. The nurse should prioritize which of the following interventions?
options: Administering prescribed pain medication
Reassuring the patient that the pain is not real
Teaching the patient distraction techniques
Assessing the patient's pain level and characteristics
quiz.rationale: Correct answer: Assessing the patient's pain level and characteristics (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

sections.title: 1. NCSBN Five Rights of Delegation & Scope of Practice

blocks.text: Safe delegation enables the RN to focus cognitive priority on unstable clients while safely assigning predictable tasks to **LPNs/LVNs** and routine care to **UAPs/CNAs**. Remember the golden **LaCharity Rule**: delegation transfers authority to perform a task, **never accountability** for patient safety or clinical outcomes.

blocks.alt: Hospital bedside healthcare team in blue PPE with NCSBN Five Rights of Delegation and RN vs LPN vs UAP scope matrices
blocks.caption: Figure 2.2: NCSBN Five Rights of Delegation, RN-Only EAT Rule, and Team Scope-of-Practice Division.

blocks.title: NCSBN Five Rights of Clinical Delegation
blocks.caption: Verify every step before assigning any nursing task to an LPN or UAP.

steps.label: Right Task
steps.detail: Task falls within legal job description & hospital policy for that staff role

steps.label: Right Circumstance
steps.detail: Patient is clinically stable, predictable & chronic (never fresh post-op/unstable)

steps.label: Right Person
steps.detail: Staff member holds verified competency for that exact procedure

steps.label: Right Communication
steps.detail: Give crystal-clear limits: what parameters to report back & exact deadline

steps.label: Right Supervision
steps.detail: Monitor completion, verify normal vs. abnormal cues & evaluate patient outcome

sections.title: 2. RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP Scope-of-Practice Matrix

blocks.title: Definitive NCLEX Delegation Scope Matrix (EAT Framework)
rows: **RN (Registered Nurse)**
Admission assessments, initial client/discharge teaching, clinical evaluation, care plan creation, unstable or fresh post-op clients, **IV push / blood transfusions / TPN titration**.
RN retains exclusive duty for **E-A-T**: **E**valuation, initial **A**ssessment, and initial/discharge **T**eaching.
**LPN / LVN**
PO/IM/SubQ meds, **stable chronic clients** (dementia, CHF follow-up), chronic dressing changes, Foley catheter insertion, trach suctioning, ostomy care, **reinforcing** existing RN teaching.
**NEVER assign to LPN:** Initial patient admission assessment, unstable vitals, blood product initiation, IV push pain/cardiac boluses.
**UAP / CNA**

Routine vital signs on **stable** clients, ADLs/bathing, ambulation, strict I&O totals, empty Foley bags, daily weights, non-dysphagic feeding, standard fingerstick glucose, urine/stool specimen transport.
**NEVER assign to UAP:** Listening to lungs/bowel sounds, feeding stroke/dysphagia patients, sterile wound care, any medication (including OTC/topical barrier creams if medicated).

blocks.title: Worked Delegation Assignment Scenarios (Unit Leadership)
rows: Client with chronic Parkinson's disease requiring assistance eating lunch & routine vitals.
**UAP** (unless severe dysphagia)
Predictable ADLs and stable vitals belong to UAP (if dysphagia risk present, keep with RN/Speech guidelines).
Stable day-5 stroke client needing routine Foley insertion & oral metformin administration.
**LPN / LVN**
LPNs perform sterile straight/Foley catheterization and administer scheduled PO medications safely.
New admission from ED with GI bleed (BP 88/52, hematemesis) ordered for packed RBCs.
**RN Only**
Unstable hemodynamics + initial admission assessment + blood transfusion require direct RN care.

quiz.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with RN (Registered Nurse) (Safe Delegation & Supervision (RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP)). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
Admission assessments, initial teaching, care planning, IV push/blood transfusion, unstable clients.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
quiz.rationale: For RN (Registered Nurse), the priority intervention is: Admission assessments, initial teaching, care planning, IV push/blood transfusion, unstable clients. Key exam watchpoint: Remain directly responsible for the EAT framework: Evaluation, Assessment, Teaching.

quiz.prompt: Which statement reflects an unsafe error (or NCLEX trap) that the nurse must AVOID when managing RN (Registered Nurse)?
options: Monitor vital signs, airway, and target labs closely during care of RN (Registered Nurse).
Admission assessments, initial teaching, care planning, IV push/blood transfusion, unstable clients.
Remain directly responsible for the EAT framework: Evaluation, Assessment, Teaching.
Use closed-loop SBAR communication when escalating abnormal clinical changes.
quiz.rationale: When caring for RN (Registered Nurse), avoiding this unsafe action is critical: Remain directly responsible for the EAT framework: Evaluation, Assessment, Teaching.

quiz.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with LPN / LVN (Safe Delegation & Supervision (RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP)). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
Oral/IM/SubQ meds, stable chronic dressing changes, Foley insertion, reinforcing existing teaching, monitoring chronic clients.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
quiz.rationale: For LPN / LVN, the priority intervention is: Oral/IM/SubQ meds, stable chronic dressing changes, Foley insertion, reinforcing existing teaching, monitoring chronic clients. Key exam watchpoint: Initial admission assessment, IV push meds, blood administration, unstable/fresh post-op clients.

quiz.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with UAP / CNA (Safe Delegation & Supervision (RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP)). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
Routine vitals on stable clients, ADLs, ambulation, strict I&O, bed-making, specimen transport, capillary glucose checks.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
quiz.rationale: For UAP / CNA, the priority intervention is: Routine vitals on stable clients, ADLs, ambulation, strict I&O, bed-making, specimen transport, capillary glucose checks. Key exam watchpoint: Any nursing assessment, sterile dressing changes, medication administration, or dysphagia feeding evaluation.

quiz.prompt: A client managed for Safe Delegation & Supervision (RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP) develops sudden tachypnea (RR 32/min), SpO2 87%, and new-onset restlessness. What should the nurse do FIRST?
options: Ask the UAP to assist the client to ambulate in the hallway.
Elevate the head of the bed, assess airway/lung sounds, and apply supplemental oxygen.
Document the vital signs and recheck oxygen saturation in 2 hours.
Administer a PRN opioid analgesic for restlessness before assessing.
quiz.rationale: Under Maslow's hierarchy and ABC prioritization in Safe Delegation & Supervision (RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP), airway and oxygenation cues (SpO2 87%, RR 32, hypoxia-induced restlessness) require immediate airway/O2 support first.

quiz.prompt: Which client care task related to Safe Delegation & Supervision (RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP) is appropriate to delegate to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel (UAP)?
options: Performing the comprehensive admission assessment for a newly arrived acute client.
Providing initial discharge teaching on red-flag warning signs.
Evaluating the client's therapeutic response to an intravenous high-alert medication.
Obtaining routine vital signs and strictly measuring oral intake and urine output on a stable client.
quiz.rationale: Per LaCharity PDA and NCSBN delegation rules, UAPs perform routine, stable data collection (vitals, I&O, ADLs), while assessment, teaching, and evaluation remain RN-only duties.

quiz.prompt: A preceptor reviews discharge teaching for a client recovering under Safe Delegation & Supervision (RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP). Which statement by the client indicates teaching was effective?
options: "It is fine to take over-the-counter NSAIDs alongside my prescribed anticoagulants without asking."
"I do not need follow-up lab monitoring because my hospital discharge labs were normal."
"Once I feel a little better tomorrow, I can stop taking all prescribed medications."
"I will monitor for warning signs like fever, worsening shortness of breath, or bleeding and contact my provider promptly."
quiz.rationale: Effective client education in Safe Delegation & Supervision (RN vs. LPN/LVN vs. UAP) requires adherence to therapy, scheduled lab follow-ups, and prompt reporting of acute deterioration.

options: Prioritize Hypotheses — ranking immediate life-threatening complications first.
Archive the admission chart without creating a care plan.
Evaluate Outcomes prior to implementing any bedside intervention.
Delegate hypothesis ranking to support staff before completing assessment.
quiz.rationale: The 6 steps of the NCSBN CJMM progress in order: Recognize Cues -> Analyze Cues -> Prioritize Hypotheses -> Generate Solutions -> Take Action -> Evaluate Outcomes.

options: Visual system
Vestibular system
Olfactory system
Tactile system
quiz.rationale: The vestibular system (B), located within the inner ear, is responsible for maintaining balance and spatial orientation. Vertigo, a sensation of feeling off balance, is often caused by problems in this system. The visual (A), olfactory (C), and tactile (D) systems are not typically associated with symptoms of vertigo.

quiz.prompt: As a nurse leader, you notice that one of your team members is consistently late for their shift. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ignore the behavior as it doesn't affect patient care.

sections.title: 1. Mass Casualty Disaster Triage (START Protocol) vs. Routine ED

blocks.text: During routine Emergency Department triage, the sickest patient (including cardiac arrest) receives maximum resuscitation first. During a **Mass Casualty Incident (MCI)** where victims vastly outnumber resources, nursing ethics shift to saving the **greatest number of salvageable lives** using the rapid **START (Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment)** 30-second color tag algorithm.

blocks.alt: Paramedic emergency response ambulance paired with Red, Yellow, Green and Black START mass casualty disaster triage rules
blocks.caption: Figure 2.3: Mass Casualty Disaster Triage Tagging (START 30-2-Can Do Rule) vs. Routine Emergency Care.

blocks.title: Mass Casualty START Color Triage Tagging Matrix
rows: **RED — Immediate (Priority 1)**
RR >30, Cap Refill >2 sec, absent radial pulse, or cannot follow simple commands.
Airway compromise (reposition airway first!), tension pneumothorax, active arterial hemorrhage, hemothorax, severe shock.
**YELLOW — Delayed (Priority 2)**
RR <30, intact radial pulse (<2s refill), follows commands, serious but non-lethal injury.
Open femur fracture with intact distal pulses, large non-bleeding lacerations, stable moderate burns (<20% TBSA non-airway).
**GREEN — Minimal (Priority 3)**
Able to walk away to safe zone ('Walking Wounded').
Minor abrasions, ankle sprains, emotional distress — direct to holding area to assist others safely.
**BLACK — Expectant (Priority 4)**
Apneic AFTER jaw-thrust airway opening, or nonsalvageable massive trauma.
Open cranial brain trauma with fixed dilated pupils, pulseless cardiac arrest in mass disaster — provide comfort/pain relief only.

sections.title: 2. Hospital Surge Bed Clearing & Acute Patient Prioritization

blocks.title: Prioritizing Across 4 Simultaneous Patients (Shift Assessment Drills)
rows: **Acute airway/perfusion shift** (thyroidectomy client with stridor; post-op day 0 BP dropping; chest pain)
**1st (Immediate)**
True systemic threats affecting **Airway, Breathing, Circulation, or Acute Neuro** demand immediate RN rescue.
**Fresh post-op assessment or new lab critical** (K+ 6.2 mEq/L, WBC <1,000, sudden blurred vision post-stroke)
**2nd (Urgent)**
High-risk electrolyte/neuro deterioration can progress rapidly into arrest or stroke expansion if delayed.
**Hospital Surge Bed Discharge Rule** (Mass disaster arrives -> need 4 beds immediately)
**Discharge Stable First**
Discharge **uncomplicated stable chronic clients or ready home-discharge clients** (e.g., cellulitis Day 3 PO step-down, mild resolved exacerbation) to free inpatient beds.

blocks.title: START 60-Second Airway Rule
blocks.text: During disaster field triage, if an unconscious victim is **not breathing**, perform ONE rapid **jaw-thrust / chin-lift** maneuver: if spontaneous breathing resumes -> tag **RED** immediately; if apnea persists -> tag **BLACK** and move immediately to the next salvageable victim.

quiz.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with RED (Immediate — Emergent) (Client Prioritization & Mass Casualty Disaster Triage). What is the priority nursing action?

quiz.prompt: Which client care task related to Client Prioritization & Mass Casualty Disaster Triage is appropriate to delegate to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel (UAP)?
options: Performing the comprehensive admission assessment for a newly arrived acute client.

quiz.rationale: The 6 steps of the NCSBN CJMM progress in order: Recognize Cues -> Analyze Cues -> Prioritize Hypotheses -> Generate Solutions -> Take Action -> Evaluate Outcomes.

quiz.prompt: A patient is experiencing vertigo. The nurse knows that this symptom is likely related to a problem with what part of the sensory system?

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a patient with suspected macular degeneration. Which of the following findings would most likely indicate this condition?

Difficulty distinguishing colors
Blurred vision
Central vision loss
questions.rationale: Correct answer: Central vision loss (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

questions.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with RED (Immediate — Emergent) (Client Prioritization & Mass Casualty Disaster Triage). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
1st Priority — Life-threatening but salvageable within 1 hr.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
questions.rationale: For RED (Immediate — Emergent), the priority intervention is: 1st Priority — Life-threatening but salvageable within 1 hr. Key exam watchpoint: Airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, active arterial hemorrhage, shock.

questions.prompt: Which statement reflects an unsafe error (or NCLEX trap) that the nurse must AVOID when managing RN (Registered Nurse)?
options: Monitor vital signs, airway, and target labs closely during care of RN (Registered Nurse).
Admission assessments, initial teaching, care planning, IV push/blood transfusion, unstable clients.
Remain directly responsible for the EAT framework: Evaluation, Assessment, Teaching.
Use closed-loop SBAR communication when escalating abnormal clinical changes.
questions.rationale: When caring for RN (Registered Nurse), avoiding this unsafe action is critical: Remain directly responsible for the EAT framework: Evaluation, Assessment, Teaching.

questions.prompt: When using the NCSBN 6-Step Clinical Judgment Model (CJMM) for a client in Course Unit 2: Management of Care — Legal Issues, Ethics, Delegation & Disaster Triage, what directly follows 'Recognize Cues' and 'Analyze Cues'?
options: Archive the admission chart without creating a care plan.
Delegate hypothesis ranking to support staff before completing assessment.
Prioritize Hypotheses — ranking immediate life-threatening complications first.
Evaluate Outcomes prior to implementing any bedside intervention.
questions.rationale: The 6 steps of the NCSBN CJMM progress in order: Recognize Cues -> Analyze Cues -> Prioritize Hypotheses -> Generate Solutions -> Take Action -> Evaluate Outcomes.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a patient who has been diagnosed with glaucoma. Which of the following statements by the patient indicates the need for further teaching?
options: "I will need to use my eye drops daily."
"I will avoid straining during bowel movements."
"I am glad I can stop taking my eye drops once my symptoms improve."
"I understand that I will need regular check-ups for my eye pressure."
questions.rationale: Correct answer: "I am glad I can stop taking my eye drops once my symptoms improve." (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

questions.prompt: A client managed for Client Prioritization & Mass Casualty Disaster Triage develops sudden tachypnea (RR 32/min), SpO2 87%, and new-onset restlessness. What should the nurse do FIRST?
options: Ask the UAP to assist the client to ambulate in the hallway.
Administer a PRN opioid analgesic for restlessness before assessing.
Document the vital signs and recheck oxygen saturation in 2 hours.
Elevate the head of the bed, assess airway/lung sounds, and apply supplemental oxygen.
questions.rationale: Under Maslow's hierarchy and ABC prioritization in Client Prioritization & Mass Casualty Disaster Triage, airway and oxygenation cues (SpO2 87%, RR 32, hypoxia-induced restlessness) require immediate airway/O2 support first.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for several patients on a busy medical-surgical unit. Which of the following patients should the nurse prioritize?
options: A patient with a history of macular degeneration who needs assistance with meal setup
A patient with a hearing aid who needs the batteries changed
A patient with a history of stroke who is experiencing sudden vision changes
A patient with a new prescription for eyeglasses who needs education about care
questions.rationale: Correct answer: A patient with a history of stroke who is experiencing sudden vision changes (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

questions.prompt: A patient with a spinal cord injury report experiencing phantom limb pain. The nurse should prioritize which of the following interventions?
options: Administering prescribed pain medication
Reassuring the patient that the pain is not real
Teaching the patient distraction techniques
Assessing the patient's pain level and characteristics
questions.rationale: Correct answer: Assessing the patient's pain level and characteristics (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

questions.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with Restraints Safety (Legal Issues, Informed Consent, HIPAA & Mandatory Reporting). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Obtain provider order (within 1 hr for violent restraints), neurovascular checks q15–30m, release q2h.
Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
questions.rationale: For Restraints Safety, the priority intervention is: Obtain provider order (within 1 hr for violent restraints), neurovascular checks q15–30m, release q2h. Key exam watchpoint: Never tie restraints to side rails (use quick-release knot on bed frame) or order PRN.

questions.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with GREEN (Minimal — Walking Wounded) (Client Prioritization & Mass Casualty Disaster Triage). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
3rd Priority — Minor injuries; can wait hours/days.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
questions.rationale: For GREEN (Minimal — Walking Wounded), the priority intervention is: 3rd Priority — Minor injuries; can wait hours/days. Key exam watchpoint: Minor lacerations, sprains, abrasions, anxiety.

questions.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with BLACK (Expectant — Deceased/Unsalvageable) (Client Prioritization & Mass Casualty Disaster Triage). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
4th Priority — Comfort care only when resources limited.
questions.rationale: For BLACK (Expectant — Deceased/Unsalvageable), the priority intervention is: 4th Priority — Comfort care only when resources limited. Key exam watchpoint: Massive head trauma with absent brain activity, fixed pupils, full cardiac arrest in mass disaster.

questions.prompt: A nurse cares for a client presenting with YELLOW (Delayed — Urgent) (Client Prioritization & Mass Casualty Disaster Triage). What is the priority nursing action?
options: Administer sedatives or diuretics without reviewing baseline labs or vitals.
2nd Priority — Serious injuries; stable to wait 30 min–2 hrs.
Delegate acute clinical assessment and teaching to UAP/CNA.
Wait 4 hours to reassess before taking any action or documenting.
questions.rationale: For YELLOW (Delayed — Urgent), the priority intervention is: 2nd Priority — Serious injuries; stable to wait 30 min–2 hrs. Key exam watchpoint: Open fractures with intact distal pulses, large non-life-threatening wounds.

questions.prompt: A nurse is providing dietary education to the parents of a child with celiac disease. Which food should the nurse instruct the parents to eliminate from the child's diet?
options: Rice
Wheat
Corn
Potatoes
questions.rationale: Celiac disease is a disorder where ingestion of gluten leads to damage in the small intestine. Gluten is found in wheat, rye, and barley. Therefore, wheat should be eliminated from the diet of a child with celiac disease. Rice (option A), corn (option C), and potatoes (option D) are naturally gluten-free and can be included in the diet.

questions.prompt: A patient with diabetes is experiencing symptoms of hyperglycemia. What is the nurse's first action?
options: Administer insulin
Check blood glucose levels
Encourage fluid intake
Provide emotional support

options: Glaucoma
Meniere's disease
Cataracts
Macular degeneration

questions.prompt: A client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is experiencing shortness of breath. What position should the nurse instruct the patient to assume to facilitate breathing?
options: Supine
Prone
High Fowler's
Trendelenburg
questions.rationale: The High Fowler's position, sitting up at 90 degrees, allows for maximum lung expansion and can help improve oxygenation in a patient with COPD.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a 6-year-old child who was recently diagnosed with asthma. Which of the following should the nurse include in the child's asthma action plan?

Instruct the child to use a short-acting bronchodilator daily

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient post bronchoscopy. Which of the following is the most important assessment before offering the patient food or drink?
options: Vital signs
Oxygen saturation
Level of consciousness
Return of the gag reflex
questions.rationale: After a bronchoscopy, the patient’s throat may be numb from local anaesthetics used during the procedure. It is essential to ensure the return of the gag reflex before offering food or drink to prevent aspiration.

questions.prompt: A child with osteosarcoma reports pain in the affected leg. The nurse has delegated the administration of oral pain medication to a nursing assistant. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
options: The nurse should administer the medication instead
The nurse should assess the child's pain before and after medication administration
The nurse should instruct the nursing assistant to assess the child's pain level
The nurse should document the administration of the medication
questions.rationale: The nurse cannot delegate the administration of medication or the assessment of pain to a nursing assistant. These tasks fall within the nurse's scope of practice. Ensuring informed consent has been obtained
questions.rationale: While all of these nursing responsibilities are important, ensuring that informed consent has been obtained is crucial. The patient must fully understand the procedure, the risks, benefits, and alternatives, and voluntarily agree to the surgery.

questions.prompt: A patient with type 2 diabetes is taking metformin. What is the primary goal of treatment?
options: Increase insulin production
Decrease glucose production
Increase insulin sensitivity
Decrease glucose absorption
questions.rationale: Metformin works by increasing insulin sensitivity, reducing glucose production in the liver, and enhancing glucose uptake in muscles.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient with a diagnosis of emphysema. Which of the following clinical manifestations would be expected?
options: Increased breath sounds
Decreased anterior-posterior diameter
Prolonged expiration
Cyanosis
questions.rationale: Emphysema is characterized by prolonged expiration due to loss of elastic recoil and air trapping in the lungs.

Restricting fluid intake

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient with chronic bronchitis. Which of the following signs would the nurse expect to observe during the assessment?
options: Decreased respiratory rate
Prolonged expiratory phase
Increased lung sounds
Absence of wheezing
questions.rationale: Chronic bronchitis is characterized by a prolonged expiratory phase. This is due to the narrowing of the airways and mucus production that obstructs airflow out of the lungs.

questions.prompt: A patient presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of sharp, severe chest pain and shortness of breath. The patient's blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, heart rate is 120 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation is 90%. What should the nurse suspect?
options: Myocardial infarction
Pneumonia

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient on mechanical ventilation. The low-pressure alarm sounds. What is the most likely cause?

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching the parents of a 1-year-old child with eczema about skin care. Which of the following should be included in the teaching?

Apply a moisturizer to the child's skin while it's still damp

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a 6-month-old infant with pyloric stenosis. Which symptom is most characteristic of this condition?
options: Projectile vomiting
Severe diarrhea
Frequent loose stools
Abdominal distension
questions.rationale: Pyloric stenosis is a condition where the opening from the stomach into the small intestine (the pylorus) has thickened and narrowed, obstructing food passage. This often results in projectile vomiting after feeding. Severe diarrhea (option B), frequent loose stools (option C), and abdominal distension (option D) are not typically associated with pyloric stenosis.

questions.prompt: A patient is frustrated and yelling about their pain management. What is the best response by the nurse?
options: "Yelling at me isn't going to help your situation."
"I understand you're in pain, let me notify your doctor."
"You need to calm down so we can discuss this rationally."
"Other patients are trying to rest, please lower your voice."
questions.rationale: Correct answer: "I understand you're in pain, let me notify your doctor." (Verified from eye and ear  QNS.docx and Saunders 9th Ed.).

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who is receiving oxygen therapy. A family member asks the nurse why the patient isn't receiving a higher flow of oxygen. What should the nurse explain?
options: The patient's oxygen levels are within the normal range
High levels of oxygen can suppress the patient's drive to breathe
The patient is comfortable and not experiencing any distress
The doctor has not ordered an increase in oxygen
questions.rationale: Patients with COPD often rely on a low oxygen level to stimulate their breathing. Providing too much oxygen can reduce their respiratory drive and lead to respiratory depression.

questions.prompt: A patient is admitted with pneumonia. The patient is febrile, with a productive cough and decreased breath sounds in the left lower lobe. What interventions should the nurse prioritize?
options: Administer prescribed antibiotics
Initiate chest physiotherapy
Monitor vital signs every 4 hours
Encourage increased fluid intake
questions.rationale: Antibiotics are typically the first line of treatment for bacterial pneumonia. The nurse should prioritize administering the prescribed antibiotics to treat the infection.

questions.prompt: The nurse is caring for a child with Hirschsprung disease. Which of the following symptoms is most common in this condition?

Constipation
Vomiting
Abdominal pain
questions.rationale: Hirschsprung disease is a congenital condition characterized by the absence of nerve cells in part of the intestine, resulting in chronic constipation. Diarrhea (option A), vomiting (option C), and abdominal pain (option D) can occur but are not as common.

Yellowing of the skin and eyes

options: "Your child should avoid crowds and people with infections."

questions.rationale: Children who have undergone chemotherapy have a suppressed immune system and are more susceptible to infections. They should avoid crowds and people with infections to minimize the risk of getting sick.

Increase calcium levels

Reduce tumor size

sections.title: 1. Fluid Compartments, IV Tonicity & High-Alert Electrolytes

blocks.text: Safe parenteral fluid resuscitation and rapid recognition of lethal electrolyte shifts form the backbone of NCLEX Physiological Adaptation. Always evaluate **IV tonicity** (`Isotonic`, `Hypotonic`, `Hypertonic`) against **intracranial pressure (ICP)**, renal urine output (`>= 30 mL/hr`), and **12-lead ECG** waveform changes before infusing potassium or magnesium.

blocks.alt: Hospital Baxter infusion pump paired with IV tonicity shifts and K+, Na+, Ca2+, Mg2+ emergency thresholds
blocks.caption: Figure 3.1: IV Fluid Tonicity Shifts and High-Alert Electrolyte Crises (US Conventional Units).

blocks.title: Parenteral IV Solution Tonicity & Clinical Indications
rows: **Isotonic** (~275–295 mOsm/L)
0.9% Normal Saline (NS), Lactated Ringer's (LR), D5W (in bag)
Expands extracellular volume without cellular swelling. **Hold LR** in severe hyperkalemia or liver failure (contains K+ and lactate).
**Hypotonic** (<250 mOsm/L)
0.45% Normal Saline (Half-NS), 0.225% NS
Shifts water **into cells** to treat hypernatremia/cellular dehydration. **Contraindicated in ↑ICP, burns, or trauma** (worsens cerebral edema).
**Hypertonic** (>375 mOsm/L)
3% NaCl, 5% NaCl, D5NS, D5LR, D10W
Pulls water **out of swollen cells** into vasculature (e.g., severe symptomatic hyponatremia/SIADH). Infuse slowly in ICU via pump; watch for **fluid overload/pulmonary edema**.

sections.title: 2. Electrolyte Thresholds, ECG Waves & Emergency Antidotes

blocks.title: NCLEX High-Yield Electrolyte Thresholds (US Conventional Units)
rows:
**Potassium (K+)**
`3.5 – 5.0 mEq/L`
**ECG:** Prominent **U waves**, flattened T waves, ST depression, muscle cramps, ileus. Give PO or diluted IV KCl (**NEVER IV push!** Max 10–20 mEq/hr peripheral/pump).
**ECG:** Tall **peaked T waves**, wide QRS, VF arrest! Give **IV Calcium Gluconate** (stabilizes heart membrane) + **Regular Insulin w/ D50W** + Kayexalate / Albuterol.

**Sodium (Na+)**
`135 – 145 mEq/L`
**Neuro:** Cerebral edema, confusion, headache, seizures. Restrict free water; severe neuro symptoms -> slow **3% NaCl**.
**Neuro:** Extreme thirst, dry sticky mucous membranes, fever, restlessness. Give oral water or slow **0.45% NS**; monitor for neuro drops.

**Calcium (Ca2+)**
`8.5 – 10.5 mg/dL`
**Neuromuscular:** **+Chvostek** (facial twitch) & **+Trousseau** (BP cuff carpal spasm), tetany, stridor/laryngospasm! IV Calcium Gluconate + seizure pads.
**Systemic:** 'Stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychiatric overtones', hypotonia. Hydrate with **0.9% NS + Furosemide** (loop diuretic).

**Magnesium (Mg2+)**
`1.5 – 2.5 mEq/L`
**Cardio/Neuro:** Hyperactive DTRs, tremors, **Torsades de Pointes** arrhythmia. Give IV MgSO4.
**Toxicity:** **Absent DTRs** (patellar reflex gone first!), RR <12/min, hypotension. Stop MgSO4 immediately & give **IV Calcium Gluconate**!

blocks.title: Potassium Infusion Golden Rule
blocks.text: Before hanging any IV bag containing potassium (`KCl`), ALWAYS confirm **urine output >= 30 mL/hr** (`renal clearance`). Never administer potassium as an IV bolus/push — fatal cardiac arrest occurs within seconds.

Vestibular system
Olfactory system
Tactile system

options: Ignore the behavior as it doesn't affect patient care.

blocks.text: Mastering **Arterial Blood Gases (ABGs)** turns complex ICU/ER deterioration stems into predictable points. Use the **R-O-M-E** rule (**R**espiratory = **O**pposite `pH` vs `PaCO2`; **M**etabolic = **E**qual `pH` vs `HCO3-`) and always verify **Allen's test** collateral ulnar circulation prior to radial arterial puncture.

blocks.title: US Conventional ABG Normal Values & Acid-Base Disorders
headers: Top NCLEX Causes & Bedside Nursing Action
rows: **Normal Arterial Values**
Check **PaCO2** (respiratory/lungs) first when breathing/opioid/COPD cues appear; check **HCO3-** (metabolic/kidneys) in DKA/shock/NG suction.
**Respiratory Acidosis**
pH **< 7.35** · PaCO2 **> 45 mmHg** (Opposite!)
**Hypoventilation:** COPD exacerbation, opioid overdose (RR <10), airway obstruction, oversedation. **Action:** Airway/O2 (88–92% target in COPD), **Naloxone**, BiPAP/ventilator.
**Respiratory Alkalosis**
pH **> 7.45** · PaCO2 **< 35 mmHg** (Opposite!)
**Hyperventilation:** Acute panic/anxiety, severe pain, high fever, early salicylate toxicity, PE. **Action:** Coach slow breathing, treat pain/fever/hypoxia.
**Metabolic Acidosis**
**Acid gain / base loss:** **DKA** (Kussmaul respirations), lactic sepsis shock, renal failure, severe prolonged diarrhea. **Action:** Regular insulin + NS (DKA), treat shock, monitor hyperkalemia.
**Metabolic Alkalosis**
**H+ loss / base gain:** Prolonged vomiting, continuous **NG suction**, loop/thiazide diuretics, antacid overuse. **Action:** Pause NG suction if ordered, replace **KCl + 0.9% NS**.

sections.title: 2. Determining Compensation Status (Uncompensated vs. Partial vs. Full)

blocks.title: 3-Step Compensation Drill Examples
rows: **Respiratory Acidosis**
**Uncompensated** — `pH` is abnormal (`<7.35`), `PaCO2` matches acidosis, and `HCO3-` (`24`) has not moved yet.
**Metabolic Acidosis**
**Partially Compensated** — `pH` is STILL abnormal (`7.30`), `HCO3-` (`16`) explains acidosis, and lungs are blowing off `PaCO2` (`29`) to help.
**Respiratory Acidosis** (Classic Chronic COPD)
**Fully Compensated** — `pH` returned into normal (`7.35–7.45`, leaning slightly `<7.40` acid side) while both `PaCO2` and `HCO3-` are elevated.
